pr_title: posix: pthread: leverage zephyr's synchronization and threading api
pr_body:
**Note: USE_NEGATIVE_ERRNO compliance failures are false positives (pthread functions return +ve errno values)**

7 commits. Please see each commit message for details.

* posix: pthread: reimplement pthread_barrier using zephyr objects
* posix: mutex: use k_mutex instead of posix_mutex
* posix: cond: use k_condvar instead of posix_cond
* posix: pthread: rework pthreads to use zephyr api
* posix: pthread: add option for pthread_create() barrier
* tests: posix: improvements to pthread_pressure test
* posix: pthread: mitigate pthread include order sensitivity 

Fixes #58856
Fixes #56163
Fixes #57232

This significantly improves the reliability of pthreads and eliminates a race condition. Additionally, with this pthreads benefit from improvements to Zephyr's synchronization primitives and threading API going forward.
pr_comments: * removed a bit of cross talk between commits 4 and 5

* use `false` instead of `0` in `bool` assignment
* remove unnecessary `*b = -1`
* change variable names `barrier -> b` to be more consistent

Wow - tough review questions @keith-packard, but at least on my desk, your code suggestions helped me double the performance on `qemu_riscv64_smp`. Thanks! 👍 

FWIW, I left a few comments in `tests/posix/pthread_pressure/prj.conf` for benchmarking purposes.

There is always room for optimization down the road as well.

> Wow - tough review questions @keith-packard, but at least on my desk, your code suggestions helped me double the performance on `qemu_riscv64_smp`. Thanks! +1

You did ask for review. Happy to ask questions based on only a vague understanding of the code and have at least one of them turn out to be useful.

> There is always room for optimization down the road as well.

Yup. From a correctness perspective, I think this series is in great shape. I'll go do another brief pass through the types to make sure they're in good shape; I think the big issues I found was mixing up offset_t and size_t. It seems to be endemic though, so maybe I just need to accept it?

Hi @cfriedt ,

just wondering if we actually planning to add all this to upcoming 3.4 release (as there is 3.4 milestone)?

> Hi @cfriedt ,
> 
> just wondering if we actually planning to add all this to upcoming 3.4 release (as there is 3.4 milestone)?

@evgeniy-paltsev - that was the plan, yes

I'll write down some performance metrics (joins/s) across the various platforms I've tested.

| board | pre | post | % | Notes |
| ------ | --- | ---- | -- | -- |
| `mps2_an385`  | 3590  |  3225 | -10 | Solid before. Solid now |
| `qemu_riscv64`  | 5250  |  5380 | +2 | Solid before. Solid now |
| `qemu_riscv64_smp`  | 4200  |  4800 | +14 | Occasional hang before. Solid now |
| `qemu_cortex_a53_smp` | 24800 | 23000 | -7 | Would regularly crash or hang before. Significantly better now |
| `qemu_x86_64`|  20500 | 23000 | +7 | Would regularly crash or hang before. Solid now |

In general my observations have been that non-SMP Qemu targets were fine before and after with a slight performance hit.

SMP targets are doing **far** better after this change and are noticeably more stable. I was not expecting a minor performance gain on some SMP platforms.

My extra `prj.conf` for these benchmarks is below, and of course mileage may vary.
```
# Note: for benchmarking purposes uncomment the Kconfig below
CONFIG_TEST_EXTRA_ASSERTIONS=n
CONFIG_ASSERT=n

# Optionally, uncomment this to only test pthreads:
CONFIG_TEST_KTHREADS=n

# If 60s resulted in hangs in `main`, I would choose 9s, etc
#CONFIG_TEST_DURATION_S=60
CONFIG_TEST_DURATION_S=9
```
@evgeniy-paltsev - please re-review when you have some time within the next day. Otherwise, @keith-packard, @jgl-meta, please re-ack when you have a moment.

I was hacking a bit this morning on the possibility of removing the barrier, but I think it's better to keep it there to be on the safe side for now.

I'll make a few changes suggested w.r.t. cancellation / coding style, but I think I'm likely not going to try any additional optimizations at this point.
I think I've addressed most comments. Tests are passing. We'll put off removing the barrier for another day.
@nashif I think you will have to merge this one.

I can do a quick respin addressing @andyross's comments if people are on-board for re-acking.

@jgl-meta if you would like to get this into v3.4.0, you may need to help to convince @nashif and @fabiobaltieri .

I'm easy either way.

There are SMP races with pthreads in `main` though, which this addresses, as well as several other long-standing maintenance issues.

If we would prefer holding off merging, I think this is at a good point to potentially investigate if the barrier is necessary and why some SMP platforms have issues when it is removed. Again, things get very hand-wavy when qemu and SMP are involved, but who knows - maybe these are very subtle wrinkles things that can be ironed-out with the odd DMB in arch code.

> @jgl-meta if you would like to get this into v3.4.0, you may need to help to convince @nashif and @fabiobaltieri .

I just need to more eyes and more reviews on this, we still have time to get things fixed up and looked at.

Eyes on the code sure, but do you think we need more experience with running code both in qemu and on real hardware? Or more tests exploring other aspects of the API?

* corrected a comment

* `CONFIG_TEST_EXTRA_ASSERTIONS=y` (in `tests/posix/pthread_pressure/`)

issue_context.title: posix: pthread: barrier functions should not directly invoke ksched.h API
issue_context.body:
**Describe the bug**
The `pthread_barrier_t` API currently exposes and uses several implementation details to the user that make it somewhat inconsistent.

Specifically, it
* uses `wait_q`s and `ksched.h` to implement a parallel threading library to `k_thread`
* does not implicitly track improvements to Zephyr's core synchronization primitives
* adds tech debt
* provides a non-standard init mechanism

Please also mention any information which could help others to understand
the problem you're facing:
 - What target platform are you using? All
 - What have you tried to diagnose or workaround this issue? Was in the process of doing the same for pthreads, mutexes, and condition variables, and noticed this had been inadvertently broken
 - Is this a regression? No, it's been present as long as I am aware

**To Reproduce**
It's more of a maintainability bug, per se, although the danger is when we are things like race conditions in threading that tend to get fixed with Zephyr's k_thread, but are (still) unaddressed with pthreads (E.g. #56163).

 The non-standard initializer is fairly obvious, `DEFINE_PTHREAD_BARRIER()`.

**Expected behavior**
Pthread barriers should behave according to spec (e.g. a barrier that had not been initialized with `pthread_barrier_init()`) should be uninitialized.

Additionally, we should layer the pthread implementation above Zephyr's public API for consistency.

**Impact**
Definitely an issue that is blocking ongoing improvements to the pthreads API and will block any conformance testing.

Since this is part of pthreads, it's in a very similar boat to #56163.

**Logs and console output**
N/A

**Environment (please complete the following information):**
 - OS: all
 - Toolchain (e.g Zephyr SDK, ...): all
 - Commit SHA or Version used: any

**Additional context**
Should be a part of the POSIX LTSv3 Roadmap

review_comments: This seems worrisome? Why?

Just to jump in on the resolved conversation: it does indeed seem like POSIX **specifies** a deadlock as the correct behavior here.  So I guess this code is needed...

FWIW: a somewhat smaller way to make sure _current never runs again is to do `k_thread_suspend(k_current_get());`.  No need to run that in a loop as it doesn't take a timeout and as an async API doesn't have a return value.
Should this check to see if `cancel_pending` is already `true`?

I've tried to maintain the logic of the previous implementation in terms of thread cancellation.

The only pace where `cancel_pending` is read from what I've seen is `pthread_setcancelstate()`

Ok, this looks right -- if `pthread_cancel()` is called on this thread while the destructors are being processed, then we'll never get to the `posix_thread_finalize()` call below. Do we want to mark the thread as not cancelable before calling `posix_thread_finalize()` so that process doesn't get interrupted mid-way?
Sounds reasonable
I put the destructor calls into `posix_thread_finalize()` and the passed the thread to terminate to that function instead of `pthread_self()`.

You can get an error back from k_thread_join() if you try to join a running thread from an ISR (but it's legal to join a thread that already exited, or to use k_thread_join() to ask if a thread is running by passing a K_NO_WAIT timeout in an ISR), or it detects a deadlock cycle (currently limited to a depth of one: you can't join a thread that joined you, but you can join a thread that's joined another thread that joined you -- IMHO this is a silly half-feature).

The former isn't applicable to POSIX, obviously.  The latter actually mimicks a pthread API feature, so IMHO it wouldn't hurt to pass the EDEADLK back to the caller.

Good point.

`k_thread_join()` and `k_mutex_lock()` trigger assertions (if enabled) when invoked from ISR context, so there is some reassurance.

> you can't join a thread that joined you, but you can join a thread that's joined another thread that joined you -- IMHO this is a silly half-feature).

Lol... is this where the inspiration for `twister` came from?
Given the use of multiple spinlocks to protect various parts of this struct, I'd love to see comments indicating which lock covers which fields.

alternatively, just use a single spinlock for all thread data; given that it looks like most state transitions involve queue manipulation anyhow, I'm not seeing how the per-thread lock will gain much performance.
There is only 1 spinlock `lock`

Seems like qid and the queue itself are covered by the global q_lock? That was where I got confused, seeing code using different locks in ways that looked like they were supposed to be protecting the same data.
